notes: In 4.4, replaced nat-instance-source-destination-check with nat-instance-bandwidth-instance-type to test the instance-size and forwarding-capacity trade-off instead of a configuration setting.

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB on-demand bills throughput according to actual read and write requests.
cards.explanation: On-demand capacity charges follow the requests processed rather than a provisioned throughput allocation. Idle read and write capacity adds no throughput charge.

cards.statement: A provisioned Amazon DynamoDB table can throttle a sudden traffic spike while auto scaling adds capacity.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB auto scaling reacts to sustained utilization and takes time to change provisioned capacity. A sudden burst can exceed available throughput before that adjustment finishes.

source.title: Managing throughput capacity automatically with DynamoDB auto scaling

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB TTL makes an expired item immediately unavailable to application read requests.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB TTL deletes expired items asynchronously. Items awaiting background deletion can remain readable, so applications needing immediate expiry must check expiration themselves.
cards.misconception: TTL expiration immediately removes an item from application access.

source.title: Using time to live (TTL) in DynamoDB

cards.statement: Amazon DynamoDB transactional writes consume the same per-item capacity as ordinary batch writes.
cards.explanation: DynamoDB prepares and commits each transactional write, consuming twice the per-item write capacity of an ordinary batch write. The extra capacity pays for transaction coordination.
cards.misconception: A transactional group of writes has the same capacity cost as ordinary batching.

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS reserved DB instance for MySQL can discount RDS for PostgreSQL instance usage.
cards.explanation: An RDS reserved DB instance requires a matching database engine for its discount. A MySQL reservation does not cover PostgreSQL usage.
cards.misconception: An RDS reservation discount carries across database engines.

source.title: Reserved DB instances for Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Amazon RDS for SQL Server offers deployments with the SQL Server software license bundled into the service price.
cards.explanation: The RDS for SQL Server License Included model incorporates the SQL Server software license into RDS pricing. A separate SQL Server license purchase is unnecessary for that model.

source.title: Licensing Microsoft SQL Server on Amazon RDS

cards.statement: Aurora I/O-Optimized bills database read and write I/O separately from instance and storage charges.
cards.explanation: Aurora I/O-Optimized has no additional charges for database read and write I/O. Its instance and storage pricing replaces the separate per-I/O billing used by Aurora Standard.
cards.misconception: I/O-Optimized changes performance but preserves separate per-I/O billing.
cards.volatilityNote: The inclusion of read and write I/O in this pricing model could change.

cards.statement: Adding an Aurora Replica within an Amazon Aurora cluster reuses the existing shared database volume.
cards.explanation: An Aurora Replica connects to the cluster's shared storage instead of creating another full copy of the table data. Adding a reader therefore does not duplicate the cluster's database storage.

cards.statement: Deleting an Amazon RDS DB instance automatically removes its previously created manual DB snapshots.
cards.explanation: Manual RDS snapshots survive deletion of their source DB instance. Retaining those snapshots can continue to incur storage charges until they are deleted separately.
cards.misconception: Deleting a database instance also deletes its manual snapshots.

cards.statement: AWS DMS can replicate ongoing changes into a target database initially loaded by another tool.
cards.explanation: A DMS change data capture task can follow an existing bulk load. Its source-log starting point must align with that load to avoid gaps or inconsistencies.

source.title: Creating tasks for ongoing replication using AWS DMS

cards.statement: An Amazon RDS reserved DB instance purchase can apply its discount to an already running matching DB instance.
cards.explanation: RDS applies reservation benefits through billing when running usage matches the reservation. The database does not need to be moved to a newly created instance.

cards.statement: Amazon Redshift Spectrum requires copying an S3 dataset into warehouse tables before querying that dataset.
cards.explanation: Redshift Spectrum queries external data in Amazon S3 directly. Keeping suitable data in S3 avoids loading another copy into Redshift tables for those queries.
cards.misconception: Spectrum requires a warehouse data load before it can query S3 data.

cards.statement: Routing same-Region Amazon S3 traffic through a gateway endpoint avoids NAT gateway data-processing charges.
cards.explanation: An S3 gateway endpoint bypasses the NAT gateway for that traffic. Gateway endpoints also have no hourly or data-processing charge, removing that NAT processing expense.

cards.statement: Routing an EC2 instance through a NAT gateway in the same Availability Zone avoids a cross-zone transfer charge.
cards.explanation: Keeping an instance's path to its subnet-based NAT gateway within one Availability Zone avoids charges for crossing a zone boundary on that hop.
cards.volatilityNote: Inter-Availability Zone transfer charging policies can change.

cards.statement: An active VPC peering connection incurs an hourly connection fee in addition to applicable data-transfer charges.
cards.explanation: VPC peering has no hourly connection fee. AWS bills applicable traffic rather than time spent maintaining the peering connection.
cards.misconception: VPC peering uses an hourly connection charge like a managed network gateway.
cards.volatilityNote: The absence of a peering connection-hour fee is a pricing policy that could change.

cards.statement: Amazon S3 charges standard internet data-transfer-out rates when CloudFront fetches objects from an S3 origin.
cards.explanation: Data transferred from Amazon S3 to CloudFront is exempt from S3 data-transfer-out charges. This exemption concerns the origin-to-CloudFront leg, not delivery from CloudFront to viewers.
cards.misconception: An S3 origin fetch is billed as ordinary S3 internet egress.
cards.volatilityNote: The S3-to-CloudFront data-transfer exemption is a pricing policy that could change.

cards.statement: Using private IP addresses makes inter-Region traffic between peered VPCs exempt from data-transfer charges.
cards.explanation: Inter-Region VPC peering carries traffic privately but still incurs inter-Region data-transfer charges. Private addressing does not remove the cost of crossing AWS Regions.
cards.misconception: Traffic is free between Regions when it uses private addresses instead of the internet.
cards.volatilityNote: Inter-Region data-transfer charging policies can change.

cards.statement: AWS PrivateLink bills an interface endpoint a single regional hourly fee across its deployed Availability Zones.
cards.explanation: PrivateLink endpoint-hour charges apply for each Availability Zone where an interface endpoint is provisioned. Expanding its zonal footprint increases that hourly cost component.
cards.misconception: One regional endpoint-hour fee covers a multi-zone interface endpoint.
cards.volatilityNote: Per-Availability Zone endpoint-hour billing is a pricing policy that could change.

cards.statement: AWS Direct Connect port-hour charges depend on provisioned connection capacity rather than actual bandwidth use.
cards.explanation: Direct Connect charges for the selected port capacity over its provisioned lifetime. Reducing traffic through the same provisioned port does not reduce its port-hour rate.
cards.volatilityNote: The provisioned-capacity basis for port-hour pricing could change.

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 waives DNS query charges for alias records that point directly to an Application Load Balancer.
cards.explanation: Queries matching a Route 53 alias record directed to an AWS load balancer are free of DNS query charges. The exemption does not remove the hosted zone's separate cost.
cards.volatilityNote: The query-fee exemption for supported AWS alias targets could change.

cards.statement: Selecting a lower Amazon CloudFront price class blocks viewers located outside its included geographies.
cards.explanation: CloudFront price classes select the edge locations used to serve content, not the countries allowed to view it. Viewers outside the selected locations can still receive the content.
cards.misconception: A CloudFront price class is a geographic access restriction.

cards.statement: A NAT instance's forwarding bandwidth depends on the network capacity of its Amazon EC2 instance type.
cards.explanation: A NAT instance inherits its EC2 instance type's bandwidth limits. Selecting a cheaper instance can reduce the forwarding capacity available to the workloads using it.

source.title: Compare NAT gateways and NAT instances

cards.statement: Network Load Balancers share Application Load Balancers' exemption from cross-zone data-transfer charges.
cards.explanation: Cross-zone traffic through a Network Load Balancer incurs regional data-transfer charges. Application Load Balancer cross-zone traffic has a different billing exemption.
cards.misconception: The Application Load Balancer cross-zone fee exemption also applies to Network Load Balancers.
cards.volatilityNote: Cross-zone transfer charging policies differ by load balancer type and could change.

cards.statement: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration can add data-transfer fees to uploads from the internet.
cards.explanation: Standard S3 internet uploads have no data-transfer-in charge, but accelerated uploads can incur a separate acceleration fee. Faster ingestion can therefore introduce an additional transfer cost.
cards.volatilityNote: Transfer Acceleration surcharges and standard upload transfer pricing could change.
